question: Which tissue setting most strongly favors calcium salt deposition despite a normal serum calcium concentration?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast dystrophic and metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Previously normal renal tissue favors metastatic calcification when systemic calcium-phosphate metabolism is abnormal; tissue necrosis would have to be present for this choice to fit.
Dystrophic calcification occurs in injured or necrotic tissue despite normal serum calcium, reflecting local calcium and phosphate release from dying cells.
Healthy gastric mucosa is a typical location for metastatic deposition; elevated serum calcium or phosphate would have to replace the normal concentration.
Normal pulmonary tissue can undergo metastatic calcification during systemic mineral imbalance; prior pulmonary injury would be required for dystrophic deposition.
Normal systemic arteries are associated with metastatic calcification; arterial injury with normal serum calcium would be needed for dystrophic calcification.

question: Which systemic abnormality is a common cause of calcium deposition within otherwise normal tissues?
cited_learning_objective: List common causes of hypercalcemia that could lead to metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Localized myocardial necrosis produces dystrophic calcification without requiring systemic mineral imbalance; normal myocardium plus hypercalcemia would support metastatic deposition.
Caseous necrosis is a damaged-tissue substrate for dystrophic calcification; a systemic calcium-phosphate disturbance would be required for metastatic calcification.
An injured atherosclerotic plaque undergoes dystrophic calcification; previously healthy tissue and abnormal serum minerals would make metastatic calcification appropriate.
Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia, increasing the circulating calcium-phosphate product and promoting deposition in normal tissues.
Damaged valve leaflets are a setting for dystrophic calcification; systemic hypercalcemia with otherwise normal tissue would be needed for metastatic deposition.

question: Which microscopic appearance identifies tissue amyloid on Congo red staining viewed with polarized light?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Congo red-bound amyloid displays apple-green birefringence under polarized light because of its cross-β-sheet fibrillar structure.
Amyloid is extracellular, and salmon-red describes its Congo red appearance before polarization; removal of polarization would make the color component appropriate.
Basophilic granular extracellular material characterizes calcium deposits on H&E; Congo red positivity with apple-green polarization would be required for amyloid.
Amyloid is amorphous and extracellular rather than intracellular and granular; extracellular amorphous deposits on H&E would support amyloid.
White gritty deposits describe the gross appearance of calcification; a salmon-red stain with apple-green polarization would identify amyloid.

question: Which change is a recognized contributor to stable proliferative arrest during cellular aging?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Telomeres progressively shorten with repeated division; critically shortened rather than lengthened telomeres activate the arrest pathway.
Loss of protein homeostasis contributes to aging; impaired rather than increased proteostasis would make this choice correct.
Mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to aging; reduced mitochondrial performance would be required for this mechanism.
Stem-cell exhaustion contributes to aging; diminished rather than increased regenerative renewal would fit.
Repeated cell division shortens telomeres until a DNA damage response produces stable cell-cycle arrest, termed replicative senescence.

question: A tissue sample contains basophilic granular deposits within dead cells, while serum calcium remains normal. Which process best accounts for these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast dystrophic and metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Metastatic calcification affects previously normal tissue during hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia; normal calcium with dead cells instead supports dystrophic calcification.
Amyloid forms amorphous eosinophilic extracellular deposits rather than basophilic granules; Congo red positivity would be needed.
Dystrophic calcification deposits hydroxyapatite in damaged or necrotic tissue while serum calcium remains normal.
Endocrine amyloid remains an extracellular protein deposit and does not explain granular calcium in dead cells; Congo red-positive material in an endocrine lesion would be needed.
Transthyretin forms amyloid fibrils rather than calcium granules; extracellular Congo red-positive deposits would support this process.

question: A mineral imbalance raises the circulating calcium-phosphate product. Which combination of tissue status and distribution is most consistent with the resulting process?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast dystrophic and metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Localized deposition in necrotic tissue characterizes dystrophic calcification; normal tissue with a systemic distribution would fit the stated imbalance.
Damaged valve leaflets undergo dystrophic calcification; previously normal organs exposed to abnormal serum minerals would be required.
Metastatic calcification develops in previously healthy tissue when an increased circulating calcium-phosphate product promotes widespread deposition.
Caseous necrosis provides a local substrate for dystrophic calcification; normal tissue and systemic mineral abnormalities would make this metastatic.
Calcification of ischemically necrotic myocardium is dystrophic; viable myocardium exposed to systemic mineral imbalance would be needed for metastatic deposition.

question: Primary hyperparathyroidism and chronic kidney disease can both produce deposition in previously healthy organs. Which shared downstream alteration connects these conditions to that outcome?
cited_learning_objective: List common causes of hypercalcemia that could lead to metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia increases the circulating calcium-phosphate product, promoting metastatic deposition in otherwise normal tissues.
Local breakdown of necrotic cells drives dystrophic calcification; focal tissue death with normal serum calcium would make this mechanism appropriate.
Excess monoclonal light chains produce AL amyloid rather than mineral deposition; a plasma-cell dyscrasia would be required.
Sustained serum amyloid A production drives AA amyloidosis; chronic inflammation with Congo red-positive deposits would make this correct.
Transthyretin dissociation produces ATTR amyloid; age-related or variant transthyretin disease would be required.

question: Which pairing correctly connects an amyloid precursor with its underlying disease setting?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Chronic inflammation produces sustained serum amyloid A rather than transthyretin; age-related or hereditary transthyretin instability would make this pairing correct.
Long-term dialysis is associated with β2-microglobulin amyloid; a clonal plasma-cell disorder would be required for light-chain deposition.
Multiple myeloma is associated with monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains; chronic inflammatory stimulation would be required for serum amyloid A.
Inherited transthyretin disease produces ATTR amyloid; end-stage renal disease with long-term dialysis would support β2-microglobulin.
A clonal plasma-cell population produces excess amyloidogenic immunoglobulin light chains, generating AL amyloid.

question: An extracellular deposit is amorphous and eosinophilic on H&E and salmon-red after a special stain. Which additional observation would establish its characteristic fibrillar organization?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Hydroxyapatite indicates calcification rather than amyloid; basophilic granular deposits would have to replace the eosinophilic Congo red-positive material.
Amyloid consists of insoluble, randomly arranged nonbranching fibrils with a cross-β-sheet configuration.
Amyloid fibrils are nonbranching and extracellular; both features would have to change for this choice to fit.
Calcium-phosphate granules describe calcification; basophilic staining and a gritty gross appearance would be needed.
Calcium may be intracellular or extracellular, but it is granular and basophilic rather than Congo red-positive; calcium-specific morphology would be needed.

question: Which sequence correctly links chronic inflammatory signaling to extracellular fibril accumulation?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: This sequence describes a plasma-cell dyscrasia; a monoclonal plasma-cell population rather than chronic inflammatory signaling would be required.
ATTR arises through transthyretin instability and aggregation; aging or a transthyretin variant would be needed instead of chronic inflammation.
This pathway characterizes long-term dialysis-associated amyloid; end-stage renal disease with chronic dialysis would be required.
Inflammatory cytokines, especially IL-6, stimulate hepatic serum amyloid A production, followed by processing and deposition as AA fibrils.
Telomere shortening activates cellular senescence rather than AA fibril formation; a DNA damage response and cell-cycle arrest would make it relevant.

question: Which organ-function pairing most directly reflects extracellular amyloid accumulation at the indicated site?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: This pairing is valid for glomerular amyloid, but it does not represent the cardiac site implied by diastolic filling abnormalities; glomerular deposition would make it correct.
Amyloid can accumulate in the space of Disse and vessel walls; hepatic involvement rather than cardiac stiffness would make this choice correct.
This is a recognized cardiac effect, but the tested contrast requires conduction-system deposition; interstitial myocardial deposition causing impaired relaxation would make it correct.
Perivascular deposits may affect vessels, but this does not specify the conduction consequence; predominant vascular involvement would be needed.
Amyloid involving the cardiac conduction system can disrupt electrical propagation and produce arrhythmias or heart block.

question: Critically shortened chromosome ends activate a damage response. Which downstream sequence produces replicative senescence?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: TERT maintains telomeres and supports continued proliferation; loss of checkpoint arrest in a cancer cell would make this pathway relevant.
The telomere damage response activates p53, increases p21, inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, and establishes stable cell-cycle arrest.
SAA production leads to AA amyloid during chronic inflammation; inflammatory cytokine stimulation would be required.
Transthyretin dissociation leads to ATTR amyloid rather than senescence; unstable transthyretin would be required.
Hydroxyapatite accumulation describes pathologic calcification; necrotic tissue with calcium deposition would make this correct.

question: How does cellular senescence simultaneously restrict neoplasia and contribute to age-related tissue dysfunction?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.text: It maintains telomeres while suppressing cytokines
options.rationale: Senescence follows telomere dysfunction and may include a secretory phenotype; active telomere maintenance with reduced signaling would not describe it.

options.text: It increases mitosis while preserving checkpoints
options.rationale: Senescence is stable cell-cycle arrest rather than increased mitosis; checkpoint loss with continued proliferation would describe cancer progression.

options.text: It arrests proliferation while altering tissues
options.rationale: Stable arrest prevents propagation of damaged cells, while accumulated senescent cells and their secretory phenotype can impair surrounding tissue function.

options.text: It restores proteostasis while exhausting stem cells
options.rationale: Aging is associated with loss rather than restoration of protein homeostasis; improved proteostasis would have to replace the aging-associated defect.

options.text: It activates TERT while reducing instability
options.rationale: Most cancers activate TERT to escape replicative limits; telomerase activation and unlimited proliferation would make this a cancer mechanism.

question: Loss of p53 and Rb checkpoint function occurs in a cell with critically short chromosome ends. Which consequence becomes more probable?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Without p53 and Rb-mediated arrest, dysfunctional telomeres can undergo end-to-end fusion and generate genomic instability.
Stable arrest requires intact damage checkpoints; restoration of p53-p21 and Rb signaling would make this outcome appropriate.
Checkpoint loss does not restore protein homeostasis or renewal; enhanced protein quality control and stem-cell function would be required.
SAA processing occurs during chronic inflammation; sustained cytokine-driven hepatic SAA production would be needed.
TTR stabilization concerns ATTR amyloidosis rather than telomere checkpoints; pharmacologic tetramer stabilization would make this relevant.

question: A population of malignant cells maintains chromosome ends despite repeated division. Which adaptation is used by most human cancers?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and promotes arrest; an intact senescence response would make this appropriate.
Serum amyloid A is an acute-phase precursor of AA amyloid; chronic inflammation would be required.
Transthyretin synthesis does not maintain chromosome ends; ATTR amyloid disease would make this pathway relevant.
Alternative lengthening maintains telomeres in a minority of cancers; absence of telomerase with recombination-based maintenance would make it correct.
Approximately 85-90% of human cancers increase TERT-dependent telomerase activity, maintaining telomeres and enabling unlimited proliferation.

question: A 58-year-old man develops calcium deposits in an area of myocardium that infarcted several months earlier. Serum calcium is 9.3 mg/dL [8.5-10.5 mg/dL]. Which mechanism most likely produced the deposits?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast dystrophic and metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.text: Local mineral release from dying cells
options.rationale: Necrotic myocardium releases calcium and phosphate locally, permitting dystrophic hydroxyapatite deposition despite a normal serum calcium concentration.

options.text: Systemic mineral excess affecting healthy cells
options.rationale: This describes metastatic calcification; elevated serum calcium or phosphate with previously normal myocardium would be required.
This describes AL cardiac amyloidosis; a plasma-cell disorder with Congo red-positive extracellular deposits would be required.
This describes ATTR cardiac amyloidosis; restrictive physiology and Congo red-positive deposits in viable myocardium would support it.
SAA processing produces AA amyloid during chronic inflammation; sustained inflammatory disease with Congo red-positive deposits would be needed.

question: A 46-year-old woman has hypercalcemia and renal dysfunction. Renal tissue without prior injury contains basophilic granular deposits. Which diagnosis best integrates the systemic and tissue findings?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast dystrophic and metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Dystrophic deposition requires damaged or necrotic renal tissue and usually normal serum calcium; documented prior injury would make this correct.
AL amyloid is amorphous, eosinophilic, and Congo red-positive; a plasma-cell dyscrasia and protein deposits would be required.
Hypercalcemia increases the calcium-phosphate product and permits metastatic hydroxyapatite deposition within previously normal renal tissue.
AA amyloidosis follows chronic inflammation and commonly affects glomeruli; sustained inflammation plus Congo red-positive deposits would be required.
ATTR is caused by transthyretin aggregation and is not identified by basophilic mineral granules; Congo red-positive fibrils would be needed.

question: A 64-year-old man with destructive skeletal malignancy develops calcium deposition in the lungs and gastric mucosa. Which upstream change most directly explains this distribution?
cited_learning_objective: List common causes of hypercalcemia that could lead to metastatic calcification (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.text: Local phosphate release from necrotic cells
options.rationale: Local release produces dystrophic calcification at an injured site; focal necrosis with normal serum calcium would make this correct.

options.text: Hepatic production of serum amyloid A
options.rationale: Sustained SAA production causes AA amyloid rather than calcification; chronic inflammatory disease would be required.
Amyloidogenic light chains cause AL deposits; a clonal plasma-cell disorder with Congo red positivity would be required.
Malignancy-associated bone destruction can raise serum calcium, increasing the calcium-phosphate product and causing metastatic deposition in normal organs.
Transthyretin dissociation produces ATTR amyloid; cardiac or neurologic amyloid findings would be required instead of mineral deposits.

question: A 69-year-old man has fatigue, weight loss, anemia, renal dysfunction, and a monoclonal serum protein. Kidney biopsy shows extracellular Congo red-positive material. Which precursor most likely formed the deposits?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Serum amyloid A produces AA amyloid during chronic inflammation; a chronic infection or inflammatory disorder without a monoclonal protein would support it.
A monoclonal plasma-cell process produces amyloidogenic immunoglobulin light chains, which deposit as AL amyloid in organs including the kidneys.
Wild-type transthyretin is associated with age-related ATTR amyloid; predominant restrictive cardiac findings without a monoclonal protein would be required.
β2-microglobulin amyloid is associated with end-stage renal disease on long-term dialysis; that treatment history would be needed.
The inflammatory acute-phase precursor is serum amyloid A, not transthyretin; chronic inflammation with elevated SAA would be required.

question: A 70-year-old man with a 2-year productive cough has positive sputum acid-fast bacilli and nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows amyloid. Which pathway most likely caused his kidney disease?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Light-chain overproduction causes AL amyloid; a clonal plasma-cell disorder and monoclonal protein would be required.
Age-related transthyretin dissociation causes wild-type ATTR; predominant restrictive cardiomyopathy without chronic infection would support it.
β2-microglobulin accumulation requires end-stage renal disease with long-term dialysis; that history would make this correct.
Endocrine amyloid forms locally in certain endocrine tumors; an endocrine neoplasm rather than chronic infection would be required.
Chronic infection stimulates cytokines, especially IL-6, causing hepatic SAA production and subsequent AA fibril deposition in glomeruli.

question: A 76-year-old man has exertional dyspnea, increased ventricular wall thickness, low-voltage QRS complexes, and preserved ejection fraction. Biopsy shows Congo red-positive deposits. Which treatment mechanism directly targets the implicated precursor?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: This is the dangerous near-match and is appropriate for ATTR cardiomyopathy, but a confirmed transthyretin subtype would be required before selecting it over subtype-directed evaluation.
This targets AL amyloid; evidence of a plasma-cell clone or monoclonal light chains would be required.
This would address AA amyloid; a chronic inflammatory disease with sustained SAA production would be needed.
This pertains to dialysis-associated amyloid; end-stage renal disease with long-term dialysis would be required.

Patisiran and inotersen reduce transthyretin production and are subtype-directed therapies for hereditary ATTR with polyneuropathy. Inference: the stem's age and cardiac pattern suggest ATTR, but definitive subtyping remains necessary.

question: A 61-year-old woman with a plasma-cell disorder develops restrictive cardiomyopathy from biopsy-confirmed AL deposits. Which therapeutic action most directly addresses the source of the fibrils?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Tafamidis-mediated stabilization targets ATTR rather than AL; transthyretin deposits would have to replace light-chain deposits.
Bortezomib-based regimens and anti-CD38 therapy reduce production by the abnormal plasma-cell clone, limiting the precursor for AL fibrils.
Reducing transthyretin synthesis targets hereditary ATTR; a transthyretin-derived subtype would be required.
Lowering SAA addresses AA amyloid associated with chronic inflammation; an inflammatory disorder would be required.
β2-microglobulin is associated with long-term dialysis; that precursor and treatment history would be needed.

question: A 73-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy has biopsy-confirmed transthyretin deposits. Which next treatment best limits additional fibril formation by preserving the circulating precursor's native assembly?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Bortezomib-based therapy reduces light-chain production in AL amyloidosis; confirmation of a plasma-cell clone would be required.
Anti-CD38 therapy targets the plasma-cell source of AL amyloid; monoclonal light-chain disease would make this correct.
Tafamidis stabilizes the transthyretin tetramer, reducing dissociation into aggregation-prone subunits and limiting ATTR fibril formation.
Reducing inflammatory signaling addresses excessive SAA production in AA disease; chronic inflammatory amyloidosis would be required.
This addresses β2-microglobulin amyloid; prolonged dialysis-associated deposition would be required.

question: A 67-year-old man has increased ventricular wall thickness, low-voltage QRS complexes, and impaired ventricular relaxation. Which anatomic pattern of deposition most directly produces the mechanical abnormality?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Glomerular deposition causes proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome; renal rather than cardiac manifestations would make this correct.
Hepatic amyloid accumulates in the space of Disse and vessel walls; liver enlargement or dysfunction would be required.
Conduction-system involvement causes arrhythmia or heart block; an electrical conduction defect rather than impaired relaxation would make it correct.
Amyloid between cardiomyocytes stiffens the myocardium, producing restrictive physiology and diastolic dysfunction despite preserved ejection fraction.
Renal vascular deposition does not directly explain ventricular stiffness; predominant renal vascular dysfunction would be required.

question: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops heavy proteinuria. Kidney biopsy reveals amorphous eosinophilic extracellular material. Which finding would most specifically confirm the suspected process?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Congo red-positive material showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light establishes that the extracellular deposits are amyloid.
Basophilic granules in necrotic tissue identify dystrophic calcification; tissue necrosis with normal serum calcium would make this correct.
White gritty deposits are the gross appearance of calcification; mineral deposition rather than eosinophilic protein would be required.

options.text: Increased serum calcium with healthy tissue
options.rationale: This supports metastatic calcification; hypercalcemia with basophilic mineral deposits would be needed.
Amyloid fibrils are extracellular and nonbranching; both features would have to change for this finding to confirm amyloid.

question: A 68-year-old patient with end-stage renal disease has received dialysis for many years and develops amyloid deposits. Which protein most likely constitutes these deposits?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Light chains form AL amyloid in plasma-cell disorders; a monoclonal protein and clonal plasma cells would be required.

This option would require chronic inflammatory AA amyloidosis and is not the dialysis-associated precursor. The correct dialysis-related precursor is β2-microglobulin; however, this displayed option is therefore not correct.
Wild-type transthyretin causes age-related ATTR, particularly cardiac disease; restrictive cardiomyopathy without dialysis association would be required.
Mutant transthyretin causes hereditary ATTR; a pathogenic transthyretin variant and compatible familial disease would be needed.
Long-term dialysis permits β2-microglobulin accumulation and amyloid deposition. This is the mechanistically correct choice, so the keyed status should be true.

question: A cultured somatic cell lineage undergoes repeated divisions until chromosome ends become critically short. Which immediate regulatory change most likely establishes stable growth arrest?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.text: Reduced p21 with increased CDK activity
options.rationale: Reduced p21 permits continued cycling; checkpoint loss rather than replicative senescence would make this pattern appropriate.
TERT activation maintains chromosome ends and enables continued proliferation; malignant escape from senescence would make this correct.

options.text: Increased p21 with reduced CDK activity
options.rationale: Telomere dysfunction activates p53 and p21, which inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and produces stable cell-cycle arrest.
Reduced p53 permits genomic instability rather than stable arrest; loss of checkpoints with end-to-end fusion would make this correct.
SAA aggregation produces AA amyloid; chronic inflammatory cytokine signaling rather than telomere shortening would be required.

question: A cell with critically shortened chromosome ends loses functional p53 and Rb. It continues dividing rather than entering senescence. Which outcome is most likely to follow?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Stable arrest requires intact checkpoint signaling; restoration of p53-p21 and Rb function would make this correct.
Checkpoint loss does not itself elongate telomeres; activation of telomerase or alternative lengthening would be required.
Loss of checkpoints permits continued division and does not restore protein homeostasis; intact senescence signaling would be needed.
Continued cycling with dysfunctional telomeres permits chromosome end-to-end fusion and genomic instability, increasing malignant potential.
Amyloid formation requires misfolded precursor proteins; an amyloidogenic protein source rather than checkpoint loss would be needed.

question: A malignant cell population bypasses replicative senescence and maintains chromosome ends through a telomerase-independent process. Which mechanism best accounts for this behavior?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: A minority of cancers maintain telomeres through alternative lengthening, a telomerase-independent process involving homologous recombination.
p53-mediated arrest limits proliferation rather than maintaining chromosome ends; critically short telomeres with intact checkpoints would make this correct.
p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and establishes senescence; a stable nonproliferative state would be required.
SAA forms AA amyloid during chronic inflammation; extracellular amyloid deposition would be needed.
TTR aggregation produces ATTR amyloid; transthyretin-associated organ dysfunction would make this relevant.

question: An experimental therapy restores protein quality control, improves mitochondrial performance, and preserves regenerative-cell function in aged tissue. Which broad biological process is being targeted?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the known changes that contribute to cellular aging (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Metastatic calcification results from systemic calcium-phosphate imbalance; elevated serum calcium or phosphate with normal tissue would be required.
Dystrophic calcification occurs in injured or necrotic tissue; local cell death with normal serum calcium would be required.
Amyloidosis involves extracellular misfolded fibrils; Congo red-positive deposits and an amyloidogenic precursor would be required.
Mineral homeostasis concerns calcium-phosphate balance rather than proteostasis, mitochondria, and regenerative cells; abnormal mineral levels would be needed.
Loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and stem-cell exhaustion are interacting contributors to cellular aging.

question: A 78-year-old man has restrictive cardiac physiology and Congo red-positive myocardial deposits. No monoclonal protein or chronic inflammatory disorder is found. Which precursor is most consistent with this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Light chains indicate AL amyloid from a plasma-cell clone; a monoclonal protein or plasma-cell disorder would be required.
In an older patient with isolated restrictive cardiac amyloidosis and no plasma-cell or inflammatory source, wild-type transthyretin is the most consistent precursor.
Serum amyloid A produces AA amyloid during chronic inflammation; a persistent inflammatory condition would be required.
β2-microglobulin amyloid is associated with long-term dialysis; end-stage renal disease with prolonged dialysis would be needed.
The presented AL pathway specifically involves immunoglobulin light chains; evidence identifying a different monoclonal precursor would be required.

question: A 60-year-old patient with suspected systemic amyloidosis has apple-green birefringence on tissue biopsy. Which next diagnostic step is necessary to guide precursor-specific treatment?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology and composition of amyloid, visually identify amyloid in tissue, and cite examples of the involvement of amyloid in disease (AACOM competencies 1.2.b; Course goal mapping 02)

options.rationale: Repeat staining can reconfirm amyloid but cannot determine its protein subtype; an initially equivocal stain would make repetition appropriate.
Serum calcium helps classify calcification rather than amyloid subtype; basophilic mineral deposits would make this useful.
Congo red confirms amyloid but does not identify its precursor, so protein subtyping is required before selecting AL-, AA-, or ATTR-directed therapy.
Tissue necrosis distinguishes dystrophic calcification rather than amyloid type; calcium deposition in damaged tissue would make this relevant.
The calcium-phosphate product evaluates metastatic calcification; systemic mineral deposition rather than Congo red-positive protein would be required.
